teaser: In 2016 you could rent this room for ten dollars a night. Van Gogh painted it three times.
review_notes:
CATALOG ISSUE: the image appears to be the FIRST version (Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam, October 1888: portraits of Boch and Milliet on the wall, pale blue walls, red blanket), not the Art Institute of Chicago version of 1889. Spots were kept to features shared by both versions, but the picture should be replaced.
Airbnb replica by the Art Institute of Chicago, 2016, 10 dollars a night, booked within minutes: check.
Left door leading to the guest room (Gauguin's): per Van Gogh Museum description, check.
First version damaged by damp/flooding while van Gogh was in hospital; Chicago copy made at Saint-Remy in September 1889; third, smaller version (Musee d'Orsay) for his mother and sister.
Walls originally violet/lilac, faded as the red pigment degraded: per Van Gogh Museum and Art Institute research.
Yellow House damaged by bombing in 1944 and later demolished.
Chicago version entered the Art Institute in 1926 (Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection).
Portraits in the later versions differ from the first (a self-portrait among them): check wording.

lesson.text: In 2016, a listing appeared on Airbnb: one small bedroom in Chicago, ten dollars a night, with a yellow bed, two straw chairs and crooked pictures on the wall. The Art Institute of Chicago had built a full-size copy of this painting that you could sleep in. It booked up within minutes.
Why would anyone want to sleep inside a painting of a cheap rented room? Because Vincent van Gogh made it look like the safest place on earth. That was exactly his plan.

In October 1888 he was living in Arles, in the south of France, in a small building he called the Yellow House. He had bought the furniture himself and was waiting for the painter Paul Gauguin to move in. After days of exhausting work, he decided to paint his own bedroom.
Van Gogh wanted this picture to rest your mind. He wrote that the colors should suggest sleep, and that looking at it should rest the brain, or rather the imagination.
The room holds almost nothing: a bed, a table, two chairs, a few clothes on pegs. His own things are here too. One of them is the hat he wore to paint outdoors under the southern sun.
Van Gogh hung up his straw hat before painting. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The straw hat
spots.text: It hangs on the last peg, just behind the bed, next to his blue work smocks. These few clothes are the only sign of the man who lives here. He painted his room, and left himself out of it.

lesson.text: An empty room, then, yet full of him. Notice also how few shadows there are. The chair legs, the table, the bed: nothing casts a shadow on the floor. Van Gogh said he had removed them on purpose and painted in flat areas of color, like the Japanese woodblock prints he collected.
The room really was crooked. The Yellow House stood on an angled street corner, so the far wall of the bedroom ran at a slant. Part of what looks like a mistake in the drawing is simply the building.

Still, the building does not explain everything. The floor seems to tip up, and the bed looks huge. Van Gogh pushed the perspective, the set of rules that makes a flat picture look deep, to bring the furniture toward you.
Two edges show how steeply the room is built.

lines.label: The side of the bed
lines.text: This edge climbs almost straight up the picture. The bed takes over a third of the room, solid as a boat. He chose that sturdy shape because it spoke to him of rest.

lines.label: The floorboards
lines.text: The boards race toward the back wall, far faster than in a real room. You seem to be standing inside, looking down at your own feet.

lines.label: The closed view
lines.text: Where all this depth should lead, there is a window. Its shutters let in a greenish light but show nothing outside. The room keeps the world out.

lesson.text: So the space is steep but sealed, and that is why it comforts. Everything in it is close at hand, big and simple, like furniture in a child's drawing. Nothing from outside can come in.
The colors you see are not quite the ones he painted. Van Gogh described the walls as pale violet. A red pigment in his mixture faded over time, and the violet turned to blue.
Count the objects and a pattern appears. For a man who lived alone, van Gogh owned a surprising number of things in twos.

spots.title: Two pillows
spots.text: Two pillows lie side by side on a bed made for one sleeper. Some see only comfort here. Others see a wish for company.

spots.title: Two chairs
spots.text: A second straw chair waits by the head of the bed, the twin of the one near the door. He had bought a whole set of chairs for the Yellow House, hoping other painters would join him.

spots.title: Two portraits
spots.text: Two faces hang above the bed. They change from one version of the painting to the next: friends from Arles in the first, other faces, his own among them, in the later ones.

lesson.text: Yes, versions. While van Gogh was in hospital that winter, damp damaged the first canvas. In September 1889, living in an asylum in Saint-Rémy, he copied it at the same size. That copy is the one that hangs in Chicago. Soon after, he painted a third, smaller one as a gift for his mother and sister.

By then the life the picture promised was over. Gauguin had come and left after two stormy months, and van Gogh never lived in the Yellow House again. He was repainting, from memory and from his own canvas, a calm he no longer had.
You cannot visit the real room. The Yellow House was hit during a bombing raid in 1944 and later pulled down. The three paintings, in Amsterdam, Chicago and Paris, are what is left of it.

spots.title: The washstand
spots.text: A jug, a basin, bottles and a brush on a plain wooden table. This corner was all the bathroom he had.

spots.title: The red blanket
spots.text: The one strong red in the room. Van Gogh listed it carefully in his letters: scarlet blanket, butter yellow bed, lemon green pillows.

spots.title: The towel
spots.text: A towel hangs from a nail by the door, striped in red. Even the smallest objects get a firm dark outline, as in a Japanese print.

spots.title: The mirror
spots.text: A small mirror hangs by the window. It reflects nothing you can read, only a patch of pale color.

spots.title: The near chair
spots.text: Thick yellow strokes for the wood, green ones for the woven seat. The paint follows the direction of the straw.

spots.title: The door on the left
spots.text: There is a door on each side of the room. This one led to the guest room he had prepared for Gauguin.

quiz.question: What feeling did van Gogh want this painting to give?
quiz.explanation: He wrote that the picture should rest the brain, or rather the imagination.

quiz.question: Why are there no shadows under the furniture?
options: He removed them on purpose, as in Japanese prints
quiz.explanation: He chose flat areas of color like the Japanese prints he collected.

quiz.question: How many versions of The Bedroom did van Gogh paint?
quiz.explanation: The first in 1888, then two more in 1889.

quiz.question: Why do the walls look blue today?
options: A red pigment faded and the violet turned blue
He ran out of violet paint
quiz.explanation: He described the walls as pale violet, but the red in the mixture faded.

quiz.question: Where was van Gogh living when he painted the version now in Chicago?
quiz.explanation: He copied the damaged first canvas there in September 1889.

facts.text: The slanted far wall is partly real: the Yellow House stood on an angled corner.
facts.explanation: The room itself was not a regular rectangle.

facts.text: You can still visit van Gogh's bedroom in Arles today.
facts.explanation: The Yellow House was bombed in 1944 and later demolished.

facts.text: Van Gogh's straw hat hangs on a peg behind the bed.
facts.explanation: It hangs on the last peg beside his blue work smocks.
